title: Senate Bill S9483 — New York Financial Data Rights Act
date_evidence:
I N  S E N A T E

                             March 17, 2026
___________

Introduced  by  Sen.  MAY
key_claim: The proposed New York Financial Data Rights Act would prohibit financial institutions from imposing any fee for making covered data available, require a developer interface, and set a civil penalty of up to ten thousand dollars per violation, enforced by the Superintendent of Financial Services.
frame_summary: The bill argues that free access to one's own financial data is a consumer right worth codifying in state banking law, explicitly countering the CFPB's August 2025 reopening of the fee question.
verbatim_quote: NO FINANCIAL INSTITUTION SHALL DIRECTLY OR INDIRECTLY IMPOSE A  FEE,  ASSESSMENT,  OR  ANY  OTHER CHARGE  TO  A  CONSUMER, SMALL BUSINESS, OR AUTHORIZED REPRESENTATIVE IN CONNECTION WITH RECEIVING REQUESTS FOR OR MAKING AVAILABLE COVERED  DATA
notes: Structural anchor (3-6 month band): the canonical primary text for the state-countermove framing. Second verbatim anchor on the page: 'SUBJECT  TO  A  CIVIL  PENALTY OF NOT MORE THAN TEN THOUSAND DOLLARS PER VIOLATION'. Companion bill A10640 introduced 13/03/2026; both in Banks Committee. title: The GUARD Financial Data Act Reflects a Misguided Pro-Regulatory Consensus
key_claim: The House Republicans' GUARD Financial Data Act would update Gramm-Leach-Bliley, pre-empt state financial-privacy laws, and bar financial institutions from blocking disclosed screen scraping.
frame_summary: Cato argues the emerging federal financial-data consensus over-regulates: data minimisation and deletion rights would impede fraud detection and AI-era innovation, and codifying screen scraping weakens banks' incentive to build secure open-banking access.
verbatim_quote: If financial service providers cannot block or ban screen scraping, they will have less incentive to participate in open banking.
notes: Think-tank counter-voice; also the in-window route to the GUARD Act development (the Act's own committee documents date to 21-22 April 2026, outside the 90-day editorial window). # Open Banking Regulation In 2026: Federal Regulation Resurfaces As States Bring Data Sharing Into Focus
key_claim: The CFPB is reported to intend a rewrite that eliminates the total ban on data-provider fees, permitting fees after a set number of free requests, while the enjoined 2024 rule stays unenforceable and states begin to fill the void.
frame_summary: Ballard Spahr argues US open banking is defined by federal limbo: the fee ban is expected to give way to tiered fees, the bulk of the 2024 obligations will likely survive, and the consequential motion is happening in statehouses and bilateral data-access agreements.

title: Open Banking Moves From Access to Economics
key_claim: The open-banking debate has shifted from who owns the data to who pays for access; a pricing-flexible federal rule could split the market into free commodity data and fee-bearing premium data services.
frame_summary: PYMNTS argues the battleground has moved from data-access rights to data economics, and that fee flexibility would force fintechs to ration requests while giving banks a premium data business.
verbatim_quote: estimates that roughly 46% of U.S. consumers are willing to use open banking payments for at least one type of purchase, with monthly bills, groceries and subscriptions drawing the strongest interest. But only 11% of consumers reported using an open banking payment.
notes: The 46%/11% figures are PYMNTS Intelligence survey data produced with Trustly; treat as trade-press survey numbers, attributed in body. # CFPB Agenda Shows Where Existing Rules May Change
key_claim: The Section 1033 rulemaking sits on the CFPB's Spring 2026 Unified Agenda at proposed-rule stage under reconsideration status.
frame_summary: Venable argues the agenda signals reassessment rather than deregulation: rules under reconsideration create uncertainty comparable to new regulation, and state legislatures and private litigation continue regardless of a thinner federal programme.

title: Open Banking Data Access Fees: JPMorgan, Plaid & the CFPB Fee Question
key_claim: JPMorgan received 1.89 billion aggregator data requests in June 2025, only about 13% tied to a customer-initiated action, and reached a paid data-access deal with Plaid by September 2025 at fees described as fractions of a cent per pull.
frame_summary: The tracker argues that data-access pricing has become a deciding economic variable for fintechs: the JPMorgan precedent established bulk bank-data access as a paid service, rewarding efficient API access and squeezing out screen scraping.
verbatim_quote: In June 2025 alone it received 1.89 billion data requests from aggregators, and said only about 13% were tied to something the customer actually did in the moment
verbatim_list: A widely circulated Forbes estimate suggested Plaid could face on the order of $300 million in new annual fees under JPMorgan's proposed pricing.
Under PSD2 (and the proposed PSD3/PSR), regulated access in Europe is broadly mandated without per-request bank fees
